data.analogy-of-the-ego-and-final-assurance#A:
The engineer designed an efficient car, but it was two inches taller than the workshop exit. The watchman suggested a brilliant solution. He advised: “You remove the air in all four wheels, let it go down by about two inches. Then take it out and then you refill the air in the tires”.
The lesson is: Release that air of ego in daily life. Your life will be very smooth. Release the air of pride which each one of us has. Just release that pride. Life will be smooth. Even for daily, smooth life, these negative traits have to be conquered. Although Pandavas were low in numbers and strength compared to the hundred Kauravas plus powerful allies like Bhishma, Dronacharya, and Karna, they won because they represented the eternal truths. Similarly, a few good habits (like interest to improve, sadhana, and meditate) are adequate, with the help of a Guru, to conquer many negative traits carried for incarnations.
Recalling Guruji’s assurance: “Each person has to fight his own battle of Kurukshetra. It is a war not only worth winning, but in the divine order of the universe and of the eternal relationship between the soul and God, a war that sooner or later must be won.” It’s never a question of whether to win, just a question of when to win.
Aum, shanti, shanti, shanti.
data.context-of-the-gita-and-the-inner-kuruks:
Let us first understand the context of Gita. When Gita was delivered by Bhagavan Krishna. For this, Mahabharata in a nutshell. Pandavas lost their kingdom in the game of dice. As a result, they had to go into twelve years of vanvasa in the forest, followed by one year of ajnyatavasa, in exile. And they fulfilled the conditions. 13 years they were away from their kingdom. And they came back after fulfilling the conditions and demanded their kingdom, which is morally and legally theirs. Their own kingdom, they demanded. But Kauravas sitting in Hastinapur said, “No. We won’t give your kingdom”. Then, having left with no other option, Pandavas declared a war against the Kauravas. On the eve of the war, when Arjuna saw the people he had to fight to regain his kingdom, he went despondent. It’s not worth fighting friends and relatives to get back this material kingdom. There is an analogy with my life and with your life. “Aham Brahamasmi” is a fundamental truth. Meaning - I am a spark of Divinity. Brahman is in me. God is in me. I’m a spark of Divinity.
All religions proclaim this. All saints declare this. We are a part of that Divinity. Divine kingdom is my birth right. Divinity is my birth right, but I lost my divine kingdom in the game of delusion. Playing with delusion, I lost my divine kingdom and I am in exile, living like a mortal. A mere mortal being, subject to all the experiences, suffering, pain of this material world because I’m a mortal now, I lost my kingdom. After many, many, many incarnations, having gone through many hard knocks, I realize that my kingdom is elsewhere. That is inside, I want that kingdom. For Pandavas, it was only 13 years away from their kingdom, but for me, it is many, many incarnations to understand that I lost my divine kingdom. I have to get that back. So now, I would like to have my own divine kingdom. That’s mine. Divinity is mine. I’m heir to this divine kingdom of love, joy, wisdom because I’m a spark of God. I want to realize that, that I am the son of God, spark of God. Pandavas, although it was their own kingdom, their mere asking was not enough.
Because Kauravas denied them their kingdom. Similarly, my mere understanding that I want my divine kingdom is not adequate because there are some Kauravas sitting in me. These Kauravas are preventing me to have my own kingdom. Who are these Kauravas? My desires, anger, pride, jealousy, ahankara, ego, habits. These are all there in me. These are all Kauravas. As long as these Kauravas are in me, I cannot get back. As long as Duryodhana, Duhshasana and other Kauravas were there, Pandavas could not get back their kingdom.
They had to be annihilated. Then only they could get back their kingdom. Same thing. Even I have to overcome my own material desires. My own anger, pride, ego, habit — I have to overcome this, conquer this. Then I will taste my divine kingdom. Just before the war, when Arjuna saw the people, Bhishma, Drona, Ashvatthama, his own uncles, father, grandfather and his own Guru, people like that, he felt that it’s not worth it. It’s not worth killing my own people to get back this kingdom. Then Bhagavan Krishna gives the advice: “People whom you are thinking “are your friends and relatives are not your real well-wishers. “They are the ones who are denying you your rightful kingdom, “so, you have to fight, you have to fight.”
Same thing with me. I want to get back my kingdom of divinity, but I understand that to get that back I have to fight my own ego. I have to conquer my own anger, pride, jealousy, my own laziness. I have to conquer these. No, it’s not worth it. I don’t know what is the divine kingdom. When I will get it? It’s okay.
But you know, I take pride in my position. In my possessions. So, do I have to give up this? Is it worth it? They are my own. They are my own. Laziness, sleep, joy that comes in sleep. These are all very happy-giving habits to me. It’s not worth it. “God Talks with Arjuna” explains that. These qualities which you are thinking are so close to you or too difficult for you to give up, are not there for your welfare. They are not there for your welfare. You have to conquer them so that you will get your real Divinity within. You will realize, God-realization. Atma Sakshatkar. What you are, you will realize only when you get rid of what you are not. My anger, anger is not me. That is sitting in me. I have to remove it. I mean, that is the analogy.
data.introduction-and-the-unique-interpretati:
Jai Guru. Love and greetings to each one of you. I’m so happy to join you all in the study of the Bhagavad Gita. Today, we have the first talk in a series of discourses on the wisdom of the Bhagavad Gita. The specific topic for today is, “Winning the Battle of Life: The Kurukshetra Within Me” based on the book “God Talks With Arjuna” the interpretation given by Sri Sri Paramahansa Yoganandaji. As we all know, Bhagavad Gita has been a perennial favourite scripture of many, many saints of various religions down the centuries.
There have been many interpretations of Bhagavad Gita. If so, is there a need for yet another translation, interpretation, “God Talks With Arjuna”? I would say that, yes, there is a need because “God Talks With Arjuna” is not yet another interpretation. It’s a very unique interpretation, as we will see during our series of lectures. This is a yogic interpretation. We have two volumes. Volume One and Volume Two running into around 1200 pages. In these two books, Guruji has dealt so much in detail, especially in terms of Yoga.
In the words of Guruji, “Yogoda Paramgurus bequeathed the world, along with the long lost Kriya Yoga, a new revelation of the Gita, relevant primarily to the science of Yoga and to ‘Kriya Yoga in particular’.” The world knows, that it is through Yogoda Guru Parampara, the long lost Kriya Yoga was revived and spread among humanity in this age. But one more thing Guruji is saying that this interpretation of Bhagavad Gita, this is also a unique contribution of Yogoda Gurus to the world. To understand Bhagavad Gita.
data.scope-and-the-grand-assurance-of-gita#Sc:
In “God Talks With Arjuna”, now, it’s vast, it has covered so much, so much. Now, from the subtle causes of everyday thoughts and actions to the grand design of the cosmic order now, daily, how I think and act, that is there in this book. Guruji represents a sweeping chronicle of the soul’s journey to enlightenment. That is your journey and my journey. To enlightenment.
Clearly outlining the Gita’s balanced path of meditation and right activity. Paramahansaji shows how we can create for ourselves a life of spiritual integrity, sincerity, simplicity, serenity and joy. Through our awakened intuition, we come to know the right course to take at every crossroad on the path of life. I mean that’s the beauty. This interpretation of “God Talks With Arjuna” is not only for God realization, Self-realization. It is also for day-to-day living, my day-to-day living, today, here and now.
Guruji wrote, “Those who study sincerely the message of Gita will find it a faithful travel companion that will not only guide and encourage, but also caution and protect.” And we’ll see that later, the truth behind these words.
And Guruji said, “I have, throughout this manuscript, endeavoured to give sufficient theoretical explanation to satisfy any intelligent layman, that yoga is indeed a science. Perfectly organised by the sages of ancient India.” Yoga is really a science, science of yoga.
And in preparing the interpretation of the holy Bhagavad Gita, my intent and prayer is to awaken new hearts and minds to the physical, mental and spiritual blessings available through right knowledge, and the application of yoga science and to encourage and hasten the progress of those devotees who are already steadfast on the yoga path. Meaning, the intent behind this book is not only to encourage new people to practice yoga, but also help those who are already on the path of yoga, newcomers as well as veterans. It’s useful for both. And any discussion on this book, “God Talks with Arjuna” is not complete without recollecting the grand assurance Paramahansa Yoganandaji gave us. This is the grand assurance:
“As God talked with Arjuna, so will He talk with you. As He lifted up the spirit and consciousness of Arjuna, so will He uplift you. As He granted Arjuna supreme spiritual vision, so will He confer enlightenment on you.”
What an assurance! “As God talked to Arjuna, so will He talk to you.” Meaning, He will talk to you and He will talk to me, because God has no favourites. He chooses those who choose Him. Meaning? He, God doesn’t want to impose Himself on anyone unless that person wants God. If we want God, we have to follow the path. He will definitely talk to us. Confer that enlightenment which He conferred on Arjuna.
And Guruji goes on, “Each person has to fight his own battle of Kurukshetra.” We all agree without any dispute. Isn’t it true? Each person has to fight his own battle of Kurukshetra, which we are doing.
“It’s a war, not only worth winning, but in the divine order of the universe and of the eternal relationship between the soul and God, a war that sooner or later must be won.” Beautifully worded, to give that assurance.
Each one has to fight it. Each one has to fight his own battle of Kurukshetra. And it’s a war, not only worth winning, it’s a war that must be won sooner or later. Let it be sooner! That means it is not a question of whether you are going to be successful in your quest for Self-realization. It’s a question of when? Each one of us, as our life is going on, we’re all seeking that Self-realization—directly or indirectly, consciously or unconsciously. Every human being is looking for that permanent joy within. That unconditional love within. Everyone! But some do that consciously, some do it unconsciously. Everyone will win, eventually. It’s a question of when, not a question of whether.
Do you know to whom this book has been dedicated? I’ll read out. “To the Arjuna devotee within every seeker.” Contemplate on these words. Gurudeva has dedicated this book to the Arjuna devotee within every seeker. That means this book has been dedicated to you, and to me because that Arjuna is in us, each one of us. So, we should be so grateful this book has been dedicated and we should take advantage. Be benefited by it.
Guruji said, “The words of Lord Krishna to Arjuna are at once a profound scripture on the science of yoga and a textbook for everyday living.” “Krishna’s message is the perfect answer for modern age, or for any age. The underlying essential truths of all great world scriptures can find commonality in the infinite wisdom of the Gita.” Gita’s mere seven hundred concise verses. The entire knowledge of the cosmos is packed into the Gita. Wherever one is on the way back to God, the Gita will shed its light on that segment of the journey. So, the Gita is useful for everyone. Beginners, veterans, or somewhere in between. Wherever you are, Gita will shed light there.
data.the-allegorical-forces-within#The Allego: So, I am also fighting a Kurukshetra war within me. And who are the Kauravas I have to fight? Duryodhana stands for material desire. He is there. Duhshasana is there, here. Duhshasana stands for anger. Karna stands for greed. Shalya stands for pride. Bhishma represents the ego in me, and the habit is represented by Dronacharya. So, these are all there. But fortunately, I also have some Pandavas in me. They are helping me. Self-control, I have. I have some degree of self-control. That is Arjuna in me. Arjuna represents self-control in each one of us. Similarly, I do Pranayama. Pranayama is Bhima. The calmness I practice, that is Yudhisthira, eldest brother of the Pandavas. And I practice the moral principles, Yama-Niyama, represented by Nakula, Sahadeva. They’re all there in me. The good qualities are there in me. So, it’s a fight between Pandavas and Kauravas. Evil and good tendencies. So, that Kurukshetra is going on within each one of us, whether we realize it or not. Because everyone wants to be good. And he knows that he has to fight, even if he’s not a spiritual aspirant. Explicitly, he is not trying for that. Meditating. But still, he is fighting his lower nature, these Kauravas in him.
data.the-author-and-authority-paramahansa-yog:
Now, about the author. This book, “God Talks With Arjuna” this was written by Paramahansa Yoganandaji. And any book, with any book we read, first, we see who is the author. Isn’t it true? We would like to know who is the author? So, now let us see who, and his qualifications to write this book. That will give us, you know, trust in the material contained in this.
Daya Mataji, our third President of our organization, she wrote, “In him”, meaning in Paramahansa Yoganandaji, “the world had been given a true exemplar of the essence of the Gita. In his active life of service for the upliftment of humankind and in his constant intimacy with God– A beloved God of unconditional love.” There are two qualities which made his life exemplary. Rather, his life, Paramahansa Yoganandaji’s life was the essence of Gita. One, that unconditional, selfless service to mankind. Two, the intimate love for God. Both, these are the ultimate qualities a devotee would like to cultivate. And he did.
That’s the essence of Gita. Service to mankind and intimacy with God. He had those two. Now, while working on the Gita interpretation, in seclusion in a small ashram in Mojave Desert, one monk said, “There was a look of incalculable remoteness in his eyes and Guruji said to me, “The three worlds are floating in me like bubbles.”” “The sheer power radiating from him actually moved me back several steps away from him.” Now, that was the state of his mind when he was interpreting the scripture, Bhagavad Gita. He was in a different world. Complete in attunement with God, Krishna, Vyasa. He was. So, the sheer power radiating it was such that, that monk had to go back. Another monk entering the room where Paramahansa Yoganandaji was working, remembers, “The vibration in that room was unbelievable. It was like walking into God.” That was the environment that was created when he was thinking about Bhagavad Gita, trying to understand and put on paper the message of Bhagavad Gita.
Guruji wrote to a devotee during that period, “I dictate scriptural interpretations and letters all day, with eyes closed to the world, but open always in heaven.” That means you’re away from this materialistic world. But he was awake there, in God’s presence. Swami Anandamoyji, with whom many of us are familiar, he said, “Several times I had the opportunity to be in the room where Guruji was working on his writings. I could see that Guruji was in a deep state of inner communion, as he put his sublime inspirations into words. So, I knew that his words did not come from intellect. They came through his direct communion with God”.
Guruji was in communion with God. He was one with Bhagavan Krishna. He was one with Vyasa, and then interpreted. Guruji said, in all his humility after finishing this book, “God Talks With Arjuna” he said, “The work is not mine, it belongs to them, Param Gurus.” “belongs to God, Krishna, Arjuna and Vyasa.” That is why he said that when he was writing this book, interpreting Gita, he was one with Vyasa, Veda Vyasa. So, he could understand what Veda Vyasa meant when he wrote this Gita, shlokas. So, that is how he was one with Vyasa. That’s why in all humility he said that it belongs to him. The interpretation. Paramahansa Yoganandaji has a dual role in this world. First, to all Kriyabans of Yogoda Satsanga Society and Self Realization Fellowship. He is their personal guru, a satguru. He’s their personal guru. And at the same time he is also a Jagadguru, a world teacher. His teachings, his message was beneficial for the upliftment of this mankind. And his spiritual legacy, is a blessing offered to the entire world, even if they’re not his direct disciples, even not their Kriyaban disciples. Practicing Kriya yoga, still they can be benefited. To them he’s a world teacher. But Kriyabans, he is their personal Guru.
data.the-battle-against-ignorance-and-the-fiv:
Now, there is one question. We are all Divine. “Aham Brahmasmi.” We are all different expressions of the same Divinity. If we are Divine, if Divinity is within us, why this trouble? Why would I go through this battle? No doubt, that is the ultimate truth. You are Divine. But our soul is covered by layers of ignorance. Layers, not one. One after another. There are layers of ignorance covering this spark of Divinity. Only when these layers of dust are removed, then only the Divinity comes out in its full glory.
So, that is sadhana. Sadhana is to remove these layers of ignorance. The soul is covered by five sheaths. Topmost cover is annamaya kosha. Then pranamaya kosha, then manomaya kosha. Then jnanamaya kosha and then anandamaya kosha. There are five layers. Guruji said, “Man being the microcosm of the universe has within him all five sheaths “matter, life, mind, intellect and bliss.” All the sheaths are there. Man alone is capable by his self-effort to remove these sheaths, to remove and get back to Divinity. Man is a special creation. He has the capacity to remove. And meditation is the most effective way to remove these layers of ignorance. Meditation is the most effective method for sheath removal.
Guruji explains, “By the correct practice of meditation the accomplished yogi, through pranayama, or life force control, unfolds the life energy sheath.” When I do meditation, I’m essentially practicing life force control, pranayama. With the help of pranayama, we get control of pranamaya kosha. “With mastery of the life force through meditation, man realizes the true nature of matter as a delusional objectification of Spirit.” That means annamaya kosha is under control.
When life force is reversed away from senses into the spine and up, the senses are subdued. When senses are subdued, they don’t send any information to the mind and mind comes in our control. Manomaya kosha is also removed by proper practice of pranayama.
“The cultivation of discriminative qualities through right spiritual action and yoga meditation gives man ultimately the ability to roll back the jnanamaya kosha, to reveal the bliss sheath, anandamaya kosha.”
data.the-role-of-the-guru-in-conquest#The Rol: One more point. Who killed Karna? Karna was supporting the erring Kauravas. He eventually was killed. Who killed him? The immediate and most natural answer is Arjuna. Arjuna killed Karna. But it’s not true. It’s not a full statement. I would say that Arjuna killed Karna with the help of Krishna. Without the help of Krishna, Arjuna could not have killed Karna. It was the help of Bhagavan Krishna, till the last moment. He helped. Otherwise, Karna would have killed Arjuna. You know, you remember the Ghatotkacha story. You remember the Nagastra. Bhagavan Krishna saved Arjuna. Same thing in me, I have self-control or Arjuna. I also have greed. So, my greed cannot be conquered by my self-control that easily. But I can definitely conquer my greed, with my self-control, with the help of my Guru. My Guru in this life is Bhagavan Krishna to Pandavas. Guru, now my Guru, spiritual Guru is Krishna for me in this Kurukshetra that is waging inside my own being. So, now when I understood that, also gives the importance of a true guru in one’s life. With his grace alone, with his blessings and guidance, I can conquer. I can conquer my lower nature, evil tendencies within me. So, when I understood Mahabharata like this, the Kurukshetra, now it’s becoming very interesting. Because it’s a daily Kurukshetra in me. It is very interesting.
data.the-three-fold-meaning-and-the-three-bod:
Now, one more description. One point from the introduction and then we go to the actual Gita. The three-fold meaning of the Gita. Material, astral and spiritual. Three-fold meaning. Material interpretation, astral interpretation and spiritual interpretation. So, man has three bodies. Physical body, astral body and then causal body. Man has three bodies. That is why three-fold meaning of the Gita, pertaining to each of these bodies. To understand what are the three bodies, in concise form, “Incarnate man is encased in a physical body of inert matter, “which is animated by a subtle inner astral body “of life energy and sensory powers.” “And both his astral body “and physical body have evolved from a causal body of consciousness.”
In this overview, the material interpretation of the Gita pertains to physical and social duties and well-being of man. See, as long as I have this body, I have some physical duties. I have some social duties. And Gita interpretation here, deals with that. How to take care of my physical duties, social duties and well-being of this body. That is on a physical plane, Gita gives guidance.
Next, the astral is from the moral and psychological standpoint, man’s character, resulting from the astral nature-born sensory and life energy principles that influence the formation of habits, inclinations and desires. See, this physical body moves around. But inside that the habits, inclinations, and desires, they come from astral body, inclinations, samskaras. And “God Talks With Arjuna” deals with that also. How to handle those samskaras? How to eliminate bad tendencies?
And finally, the spiritual interpretation is from the perspective of the divine nature and realization of the soul. That is Self-realization, meditation. That is also dealt with, in the same book.
Guruji said, “Hence, while I have emphasized the spiritual aspects of the Bhagavad Gita, the material and psychological import has also been interwoven, to stress the need for practical application of the Gita wisdom in all phases of life.” “Truth is of all-round benefit to man.” So, physical, astral and spiritual interpretation. It is all-round benefit to man. Analyzing the First Shloka: Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya Now, we’ll go to the first shloka. All this explanation so far, is only introduction to “God Talks With Arjuna”. Now, we’ll take shloka after shloka and understand the meaning. First, let us listen to the first shloka of the first chapter, sung by Swami Vasudevanandaji.
[Swami sings Gita Shloka.]
The plain meaning of this shloka is, Dhritarashtra spoke, “On the holy plain of Kurukshetra, gathered together, eager for battle, fought my children, the Kurus and the Pandavas. What did they, O Sanjaya?”
It’s a very simple meaning. You know, Dhritarashtra, who was the father of Kauravas, was blind. He wanted to know what’s happening on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, but he cannot see. Vedavyasa was ready and offered divya-drishti to him, by which he could see what is happening on the battlefield. But, Dhritarashtra refused to have that gift, saying that, “Even if you give me that gift, I will not be able to recognize who is who, because I’m born blind”.
Then Vedavyasa gave that power of divya-drishti to Sanjaya, who was a charioteer of Dhritarashtra, who was his companion. So, Sanjaya would see, from wherever he was, in the palace, what was happening on the battlefield and narrate to Dhritarashtra. Now here, there is an analogy. Dhritarashtra represents the blind mind in me. Because my mind is blind, it depends on senses for information. Whatever is brought through eyes, mind tries to process. Whatever it brings through ears, mind tries to process. It depends on senses for its information. If senses bring wrong information, it interprets wrongly. For instance, I see some horse somewhere. But it may not be a horse. It may be a cow. From a distance, I could not distinguish. But mind thinks it’s a horse. So, mind is blind, it depends only on senses for all information.
Here, Sanjaya was given that power, divya-drishti, and Sanjaya represents, introspection. In daily life, we have to introspect. Not only Dhritarashtra is in me, the blind mind, I also have Sanjaya in me, that is introspection. The capacity to introspect, that is there in me, Sanjaya is in me.
So, we have to ask Sanjaya, “Today, in the battlefield of my life, how did my good tendencies and bad tendencies fare? What did they do today?” Like Dhritarashtra was asking, “How did Kauravas and Pandavas do today on the battlefield? What did they do?” Similarly, my mind every day has to ask my introspection, “How did you fare?” Your evil tendencies, rather, my evil tendencies and my good tendencies.
See, this shloka, is very simple. Dhritarashtra is asking “What’s happening?” And many interpretations of Bhagavad Gita dismiss this shloka in one paragraph or one page. This is what Dhritarashtra asked and go to the second shloka. But Guruji has taken 45 pages to explain the import of this. The Kurukshetra within. The first shloka tells us a fundamental truth. “That life is a series of battles between Spirit and matter, between knowledge and ignorance, between soul and body. Battle between self-control and temptation, discrimination and the senses.” Each one of us is going through this battle inside, between knowledge and ignorance. The human body is a veritable battleground.
It’s a Kurukshetra field, human body. War between wisdom and ignorance, between wisdom and conscious delusive forces. “Every spiritual man wants to defeat rebel, King Ego and its powerful sense allies and establish the rule of King Soul in the bodily country.” Now, the import is this. Every night before sleep, a sincere sadhaka, like you, must honestly introspect, “How did I do today?” Your own introspection, that has to be invoked and it has to guide you. People write diaries. Normally diary gives, “What did I do today?” But a spiritual person goes into minute detail. He will write, “Why did I do what I did?” Why did I do, with the reason behind my actions, is also important.
data.the-three-plains-of-kurukshetra#The Thre:
The battle of Kurukshetra described in the Gita is the effort required to win the battles in all portions of the bodily kingdom. There are three main battles, or plains of Kurukshetra:
The Sensory Plain of Kurukshetra: This involves the material and moral struggle between good and evil, right and wrong actions on the bodily plane. We must be careful not to choose wrong or evil actions brought through the senses (eyes, ears, tongue),.
The Cerebrospinal Plain of Dharmakshetra Kurukshetra: This is the “psychological war waged in yoga meditation on the cerebrospinal plain of Dharmakshetra Kurukshetra.” When meditating, we reverse the flow of current in the spinal and cerebrospinal area, fighting psychological likes and dislikes and samskaras,.
The Cerebral Plain of Dharmakshetra: This is the “spiritual battle fought in deeper meditation and the cerebral plain of Dharmakshetra to overcome the lower states of consciousness and dissolve all egoity and sense of separation from God.” The guidance in the Bhagavad Gita is not only for God-Realization, but also for physical and mental well-being. It teaches how to be happy now and here and lead a joyous and purposeful life.
data.understanding-bhishmas-allegorical-faili:
Now, before we go further, I want to express my personal appreciation for this interpretation, “God Talks With Arjuna.” As a child, I liked Mahabharata story, very deeply. I always liked it. Because there are so many characters and there are plots and counter-plots and always exciting, thrilling, you know. I have seen so many books and I have seen so many movies and even children’s books. Many books I read on Mahabharata because I used to like it. Later, as I became an adult, especially after stepping my foot on spiritual path, I found, Mahabharata is the most saddest story, one can think of. Very sad story. What is it? From the beginning, even young children, fighting each other. That jealousy. That pride, that anger. Even young children, Kauravas and Pandavas. And then it went on and on. Eventually, what? A terrible war broke, Kurukshetra. And son fighting father, friend fighting friend, teacher fighting his student, like that. It was so sad for me. But, after I read “God Talks With Arjuna”, then my ideas changed. And my good feelings about Mahabharata came back. The reason is this. See, why Bhishma was killed? Bhishma was probably the most venerable person in Mahabharata. Blameless. Bhishma—Sacrifice and commitment, dedication to his kingdom.
Such a great personality. Why he was killed? And earlier, it was pain for me. But, now I can understand. No doubt, Bhishma was a very great person. So much sacrifice, so much will-power. But he had one bad quality. One bad quality. That was, he always wanted Kauravas and Pandavas, his own grandchildren, to live together in peace. There is nothing wrong in having that desire, to have his children live in peace. Nothing wrong with that. But, he has, you know, so many times he saw the Kauravas trying to disturb and cause problems to the Pandavas. All along, from childhood all the way, when they grew up, grew up, grew up. And by wrongful means they snatched their kingdom. And they don’t want to give back their kingdom. Like that many, many, many things. They tried to kill them, in many ways. So, they were erring and Bhishma knew that. If only he wanted justice. If only he wanted real peace. With one arrow, he could have annihilated the entire erring Kaurava clan. He didn’t. Till the end, even after the war was declared, still he was wanting both to live peacefully. It doesn’t happen. It won’t happen. Same thing with me. See, I have Pandavas in me. I have the habit of meditation, I have the devotion, I have the desire to serve God and love God. All these good qualities are there, definitely. But I also have some beautiful negative qualities. Like anger, laziness, pride. These things I don’t want to leave. I want to hold onto them and I want to hold onto good qualities and both should co-exist and I should get God. You know? Without leaving these evil tendencies, I want God. Like Bhishma, he didn’t want to leave Kauravas, but he wanted peace. Same thing. It will not happen. My ego, if it doesn’t leave that pride, it doesn’t leave those evil habits, laziness. I can’t get back my Divinity within. That is why for Pandavas to win, first, Bhishma had to go. He had to go. Then one by one, they conquered other warriors. Dronacharya, Karna, Duryodhana, Duhshasana. Everyone was conquered afterwards. Ego had to go. Bhishma had to go. Similarly, in me, I have to subdue my ego. My pride, my desire. I have to subdue if I want Divinity, which is mine. So, now I got interested. This is what Guruji explained. Kauravas are in you. This is Mahabharata. So, now I am not so interested in that Kurukshetra which took place 3000 years ago out there in Haryana. I’m more interested in the Kurukshetra that is taking place here, within me. All the time. I’m more interested in this.

data.advice-on-daily-practice#Advice on Daily:
Now, I would like to share with you a piece of advice I received from a friend of mine, when I just started meditation — that was about forty-two years back, 1979. I just started, a friend of mine gave this advice. “Never think whether to meditate or not. Just sit down and meditate.”.
If you think whether to meditate or not, immediately, you have a very pleasant advice coming from within. “You are too tired. You had a long day today. Others are waiting for common dinner. And, there is a serial on the TV, and you have to make a telephone call to a friend, right now, do it. Guruji will understand. You can compensate by a long meditation tomorrow. Tomorrow you can skip”. So many advices will come, if you think whether to meditate or not. Interestingly, I never think whether to eat or not. I eat, a little late, a little early, little more or little less, I eat. I never think whether to sleep or not, I sleep. But, when it comes to meditation, there’s an option, whether to meditate or not?. Why should that be?. When you get up in the morning, either before bath or after bath, meditate. We have to meditate. It should be so much ingrained in us, that habit — that means, Dronacharya. Drona is helping us. Dronacharya will help us; the same habit can help us.
A devotee I know personally had a contract, a pact with Guruji. He would say, “Guruji, regularity at meditation is my responsibility, but going deep into meditation is your responsibility.”. We don’t have control over the depth of meditation. That’s why he said, “Regularity at meditation is my responsibility, but going deep into meditation is your responsibility.”. And the same devotee, with tears of gratitude, after years he said, “I have always received more than what I expected, more than what I needed, more than what I deserved.”. “My only effort was regularity. I was regular, I received so much.”. Dronacharya. Make use of that habit.
data.habit-as-an-ally-the-importance-of-regul:
But there is hope. There is hope. Because Dronacharya was the guru of not only Kauravas, He was also the guru of Pandavas. Dronacharya trained both Pandavas and Kauravas, meaning habit could be a bad habit or it could be a good habit. Habit also could be a good habit. Take advantage of that.
Dronacharya, by force of circumstances, had to fight for Kauravas. But in his heart of hearts, he wanted victory for Pandavas. Although he wasn’t fighting for them, fighting against them, he wanted their victory, because that’s truth. Similarly by nature, each one of us, we would like to be good. We would like to side with our soul nature rather than these materialistic pleasures. So inside that is there. If only we realize that and take advantage of that inner urge to be good, we will win the battle. And same Dronacharya will help us, same Habit will help us. So take advantage of that Habit, Dronacharya. See what is habit in meditation? It is regularity. The importance of regularity in meditation cannot be over-emphasized. Many devotees do not continue with meditation because of that, because of lack of regularity. Regularity is very important especially in meditation.
Paramahansa Yoganandaji said: “The most destructive shaft of maya, delusion is unwillingness to meditate, for by this attitude, one prevents himself from tuning with God and guru.”. That is most, most destructive influence of maya – unwillingness to meditate. If somehow that unwillingness, delusion puts in me there itself, I am gone. So, we should never fall prey to this unwillingness.
Daya Mataji said, “If you are not regular at meditation, you will be a beginner even after twenty years.”. Mark her words. And this is valid for so many devotees we are seeing around. “If you are not regular at meditation, you will be a beginner even after twenty years.”. Same questions when you start; after five years, after ten years, fifteen years, twenty years, same questions because they are not regular. If you are not regular, you know how to handle thoughts, how to subdue the thoughts. That is possible with regularity.
data.introduction-and-context-review#Introduc:
Greetings! Loving pranams to all of you. I’m so happy to be with you all once again to resume our study of the Bhagavad Gita as interpreted by Paramahansa Yoganandaji in his book, “God Talks With Arjuna.”. In the first discourse we had, we could cover only the first sloka of the first chapter. Before we go to the second sloka, I would like to briefly review what we discussed last time in order to pick up the thread of continuity. To understand Bhagavad Gita, we have to understand the context of the Gita.
Pandavas lost their kingdom in the game of dice. Consequently, they had to go into exile—twelve years of aranyavas in forest, followed by one year of agnyaatavas. One year they had to spend in disguise. And they did that. Thirteen years they spent and they came back and demanded their kingdom, which belonged to them morally and legally. But Kauruvas denied them. Having no other option, Pandavas declared a war to reclaim their own rightful kingdom. On the eve of the war – Kurukshetra, Arjuna goes despondent after seeing the people he had to fight. His own people he had to fight. At that time, Bhagavan Krishna gives this advice — Gita.
data.review-and-conclusion#Review and Conclus:
Now, let us just review what we have done today. After reviewing what we said in the last talk, we went to second sloka where Duryodhana, having surveyed the armies of Pandavas and approached his guru, Dronacharya, and spoke. That is when a devotee starts meditating, the material desire in him gets alarmed. So [Desire] tries to dissuade the devotee by bringing into his mind all those past memories of habits, those pleasures he used to get. So beware, beware. Take advantage of this habit by cultivating good habits like regularity in meditation. Then Dronacharya is going to help you rather than helping Kauravas. That’s the second sloka.
Third sloka is Pandavas are helped by Dhrishtadyumna as the commander-in-chief. Dhrishtadyumna was born to kill Dronacharya, the habit. So, the bad habits in me are going to be killed. For that, we have to cultivate or generate Dhrishtadyumna — that is calm inner light of intuitive awakening by meditation practices. Then we’ll have the power to conquer whatever bad habits we have. This is for today.
Next time we’ll take up slokas four, five, and six. Pandavas were only five. Eventually they won the battle of Kurukshetra, not by themselves — they needed help of many supporters, many allies. Similarly, my, a few good qualities, like yama-niyama, pranayama, self-control, calmness — alone may not be adequate to win this battle. I also need the help of some supporting qualities like discriminative intelligence. I need devotion. I need vairagya, dispassion. All these qualities also I need in order to win the ultimate battle of delusion. So that’s what we’ll discuss — what are the other good spiritual qualities we have to develop in order to win this Kurukshetra within. That will be topic for the next talk. Okay. A few moments of silence and then we leave. Aum. Shanti. Shanti. Shanti.
Jai Guru.
data.the-alarm-of-material-desire#The Alarm o:
Ordinary person, knowing nothing of the intoxicating joy that can flow from meditational practices innocently reconciles to sense pleasures. I mean, how true it is?. Many many people are not aware what joy meditation can give on a regular basis. They’re not aware. In the absence of that knowledge that can come knowledge of joy that can come from meditation, the person reconciles to whatever sense pleasures he can have.
But when man starts meditation and gets that joy, you know, he becomes more and more interested in meditation then, the King Material Desire in me gets alarmed. “Oh! This man is now going towards meditation. That means, I may be deprived of my joys, my sense pleasures”. That desire, which was enjoying the pleasures coming from ears, and eyes and tongue. “Oh, I may be deprived”. It gets alarmed and turns towards past habit, Dronacharya – it turns. Devotee, beware!. As soon as the spiritual aspirant tries to meditate and rouse the powers of self-control and discrimination, he will find King Material Desire tempting him in several ways to distract him from meditation. When he wants to meditate, sincerely someone wants to meditate immediately he remembers: “Oh! I have to call my friend. I promised. Let me call now”. “There’s an excellent movie going on in the neighbouring theatre”. There’s a very interesting TV show – serial is going on!. Or “others are waiting for dinner”. “Let me get through all these duties. Later I can meditate”.
When all those things come to mind, these are the tempting by maya. We lost our divinity in the game of delusion. That delusion is even now working. When you want to meditate, all these things come to mind past habit – past things you have been doing it. And this is not only for spiritual aspirants, This is happening for students too. Only when a student sits for studies then he remembers about the TV program or about his friends. Even the resolute devotee who resists these lures outwardly, resists and sits in meditation, then comes inner urges of past bad habits like restlessness, sleepiness, mental sloth. mental sloth meaning laziness, because meditation is intense activity. I won’t even say that meditation is an activity.
Meditation is intense activity. Lot of effort is required. The restless man who doesn’t cultivate spiritual discrimination and self-control becomes a victim of Duryodhana, Material Desires, temptations and of Drona samskaras, inner urges of past habits of spiritual indifference and sense pleasures. For example: Sleep gives me so much joy!. It’s so easy to sleep than to do meditation. If I go to meditation, I may not get what I expect immediately. It’s not instant gratification of senses in meditation. It takes time, whereas here instant — if I sleep, I get rest. If I go to a movie, I kill time. That’s all what I want – instant!. But meditation is work.
Pure enjoyments of senses. Experience with the spiritual discrimination and self-control are not enslaving. It doesn’t mean that a spiritual aspirant, a true devotee, should not indulge in sense pleasures. No!. We can involve in all these things. We can even watch TV. We can take food, but with some self-control. Some discrimination should be there. How much? How long?. If there is discrimination, self-control, all these things, pleasures, meant for senses, satisfying senses, they are all okay. They are good. But have that discrimination. Thus, we find the second sloka of the Gita forewarning the spiritual aspirant that King Duryodhana, Material Desire, will try to arouse man’s Drona, sense-habit tendencies to fight against the soul’s forces of discrimination.
data.the-bird-and-the-rod-analogy#The Bird an:
Now, how do we conquer our habits, bad habits?. Wrong thinking, or idle thinking — that’s a bad habit. I have an analogy. A hunter normally catches birds by casting a net. But there is one bird which cannot be caught by a net. This hunter uses a very intelligent trick to catch it. He puts a rod on two hinges on the branch of a tree. This particular bird, when it comes and it lands on the rod, the rod turns on the hinges. When it turns, the bird goes upside down. And it thinks that if it leaves the rod, it’ll go and hit the ground and die. It’s afraid. It catches so fast that it doesn’t want to leave the rod, although it has the capacity to leave the rod and fly into safety before it touches the ground. It never leaves the rod and the hunter comes and catches it.
Same thing with us. I’m now hooked to a bad habit. I think that I can’t survive by leaving it. We think, I can’t live without this. But you can!. You have that capacity, being divine. You are a spark of Divinity. You have that capacity to fly into freedom before you hit the ground. You have that capacity to leave this bad habit which is troubling you again and again. It’s possible.
When will you leave? When that awakening comes. The awakening comes, intuitive awakening. Yes. Now I can leave. If I — if I don’t leave, this is what is going to happen to me, my life. Let me leave this rod, let me leave this habit and fly into freedom. Let us have that calm inner light of intuitive awakening generated by meditation. Meditation is there again, that is the solution. Then we can definitely kick the habits, definitely one by one, one by one.
data.the-elephant-analogy#The Elephant Analog:
Here is an analogy and how the habit helps — the positive habit, good habit helps, especially in spiritual practices. One king had, you know, a battalion of elephants. There was one elephant, which was very efficient at war. It won many a battle for the king, but with time it was becoming old. The king retired that elephant. One day, that elephant went to a pond. After taking water before it came back, it got stuck in the mud of that pond. They put a rope around it, tried to pull it. Other elephants also tried to pull it. It couldn’t come. More and more, it was getting stuck and going into the mud.
Then, one monk advised, “King, you please bring war drums and blow them.”. Hearing this war cry, the elephant pulled out of the mud and started running on its own. It couldn’t come out even with the help of others but once it heard the war drums, now, it got all that enthusiasm, war cry, and came out of it because it was made for that, war. It was — that habit was there. Once it heard war drums, it was ready to fight.
Same thing with us. We should have that habit. It is like a war cry, need for meditation. That’s a war cry, “I have to go for meditation.”. When the thought comes, “meditation,” you get up, alarm or no alarm. If you don’t have the urge to go for that war in meditation, then alarm is not going to help you. Now this is time for meditation. Alarm is indicating — get up, war cry. That kind of habit should be there. Dronacharya is helping you, Pandavas, cause habit of meditation is a good one, good habit, positive habit. Cultivate that. The Third Sloka: The Calm Inner Light of Intuitive Awakening Now, we’ll go to third sloka. The plain meaning: Duryodhana said. “O Teacher, behold this great army of the sons of Pandu, arranged in battle order by thy talented disciple, the son of Drupada.”.
In third sloka, he says: “Acharya — O teacher, behold this great army of Pandavas arranged in the battle by the son of Drupada,” — that is Dhrishtadyumna, that much only. Here, there is deep spiritual significance for you and for me. Dhrishtadyumna was the commander-in-general for Pandavas. The material desire in me (Duryodhana), when it observes that I am going toward spiritual practices, addresses habit (Dronacharya): “Behold the mighty army of Pandavas, the discriminative forces entrenched in the spiritual centres, all poised for battle under the direction of thy disciple Dhrishtadyumna, the calm, inner light of intuitive awakening.”.
Dronacharya represents habit. Habit cannot easily be conquered once it is formed. It is so strong, so difficult to remove it. Metaphysically saying that any habit can be completely removed by calm inner light of intuitive awakening — that has to come, that intuitive awakening should come from within. That can only destroy habit. Eventually, Dronacharya was killed by Dhrishtadyumna.
Dhrishtadyumna was the son of Drupada. Drupada represents dispassion — meaning vairagya for material enjoyment resulting from deep spiritual fervour and divine devotion. Drupada represents vairagya — that means dispassion for material enjoyments. So, that can only give this intuitive awakening within me, and that in turn can overcome a bad habit. There we need inner awakening.
How do you get that inner awakening? By deep meditation. That inner awakening when it comes, it comes with a calm, inner light. It can foresee — this is what is going to happen in the future if you continue with this habit. It can intuitively feel, this is what is going to happen, now I have to remove it. That kind of strength comes from meditation practices.
data.the-first-sloka-life-as-a-series-of-batt:
Then first sloka. First sloka, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya: “On the holy plain of Kurukshetra, gathered together, eager for the battle my children, Kauravas and Pandavas, what did they, O Sanjaya?”. That’s the question put by Dhritarashtra, who was blind; he cannot see. So he asked his charioteer, Sanjaya, who was given that vision to see what was happening on the battlefield. Although he’s sitting in the palace, but he had that vision; He was granted that vision by Vedavyasa to see and narrate to blind King Dhritarashtra. So he asks, “What did Kauravas and Pandavas do on the battlefield?”. See, the first sloka tells us a fundamental truth – that life is a series of battles. between Spirit and matter, knowledge and ignorance, soul and body, self-control and temptation. It’s all the way, all along — series of battles between good and bad, temptations and self-control, knowledge and ignorance – series of battles. And each night, a sincere devotee must see in minute detail, how did he fare on that day in the battlefield of Kurukshetra within himself. One should see how did my good tendencies behave today and how my evil tendencies behave today. We have to see!. Now it may appear to be like writing a diary. No, it’s much more than that. Normally a diary mentions “What I did that day?”. But here a devotee should introspect “Why did I do, what I did today?”. What was the motive behind my actions, my behaviour, that is also important. Not only my actions, but even the motives are important if we are to progress spiritually. That is the import. Each day introspection should come into play.
Sanjay represents – introspection. Introspection has to give the account to Blind Mind. Mind cannot see. It can only interpret the information that’s coming from the senses.
data.the-five-sheaths-koshas-and-meditation#T:
Next we have seen, “Why should I have all these struggles, trouble? I am divine. I am a spark of divinity. Then why do I go through these struggles? Why even I commit some mistakes?”. That’s the question!. No doubt Divinity is within each one of us. But the soul is covered by layers of ignorance – layers of ignorance. See, I’m covered – my soul is covered by five layers: the topmost being annamaya kosha, meaning matter sheath, matter cover. Below that is pranamaya kosha, life sheath. Then manomaya kosha, mind. Then jnanamaya kosha, discriminatory. And then anandamaya kosha. These are five covers, you know, which are hiding my soul. So it takes effort to remove these covers, and that effort means struggle. There is a battle to remove cover after cover, so that when they are all removed, the pure soul merges in God. For this, meditation is the most effective way to remove these covers; because meditation involves pranayama, meaning prana-yama – control of life force.
When we are controlling life force, the life sheath comes under our control – that is removed. When it is removed one understands that when we have control over the force, we understand that this body is nothing but just delusory objectification. that is annamaya kosha, matter sheath also is revealed. And when life force comes under control, then senses are subdued.
Normally life force goes downwards along the spine and outward from the chakras. When they go outward from chakras, they go to senses and they energize them making them active. When we reverse this, – control of the life force means reversing the flow of life force, that is, from the senses draw them into chakras and take them upwards, rather than downwards and outwards, it becomes inward and upwards. That when senses are deprived of that life force they become subdued. and the mind doesn’t receive information from the senses. Mind comes under our control, not in the control of the senses. So, the mind sheath is rolled back. Then comes to surface jnanamaya kosha. Man is mainly guided by the discrimination – jnana is discrimination. And further sadhana removes that sheath and man lives in bliss, ananda, because he’s covered by only anandamaya kosha, bliss sheath. And further sadhana removes even that anandamaya kosha – bliss sheath, so that the soul merges in — merges with Spirit, God. See, the sheath removal is not automatic. After a few years this is gone, after a few more years that is gone. No! It’s a struggle. It’s effort. That is the Kurukshetra. The Three Planes of Struggle
And here, this is happening at — There are three fields:
The Material and Moral Struggle (Sensory Plain of Kurukshetra): This is the struggle between good and evil, right and wrong actions, and on the sensory plain of Kurukshetra. If you recall the sloka, it says, “Dharmakshetra Kurukshetra” – the Dharmakshetra Kurukshetra. Kurukshetra refers to the sensory plain of Kurukshetra where the struggle is between good and bad, right and wrong actions. That is bodily plain.
Psychological War (Cerebrospinal Plain of Dharmakshetra Kurukshetra): This is the psychological war waged in yoga meditation on the cerebrospinal plain of Dharmakshetra Kurukshetra. Because in this cerebrospinal plane which is known as ‘Dharmakshetra Kurukshetra’ there are inclinations, good inclinations, bad inclinations, samskaras — they fight. That Kurukshetra is taking place.
Spiritual Battle (Cerebral Plain of Dharmakshetra): This takes place on the cerebral plain, cerebral plain – that’s higher – that is Dharmakshetra, where we fight with our lower nature in order to conquer it and get back to God. So, these are the three planes: bodily plain, then cerebrospinal plain, and then cerebral. Kurukshetra, Dharmakshetra-Kurukshetra, then Dharmakshetra. And by now, you must have understood and got convinced that this guidance given by Bhagavad Gita is not only for ultimate self-realization — the goal of life. It is also useful, here and now, to lead a joyous purposeful life. That’s the beauty of Gita, it’s useful for everyone whatever may be his level of progress in spirituality. It’s useful there. So that is a short recall of what we discussed in the first talk.
data.the-metaphysical-analogy-the-kurukshetra:
There is an analogy here with my own life and with your own life. because “Aham Brahmasmi” — I am divine. I’m a spark of divinity as you are, he and she, everyone. We are all different expressions of the same divinity, but that divine kingdom within me I lost in the game of delusion. As Pandavas lost in the game of dice, I lost my divine kingdom in the game of delusion. Having lost my divinity, I’m living in exile as a mere mortal, moving around, forgetting about my divine heritage.
For Pandavas, it was only thirteen years of exile. But for me, not just thirteen years, not just thirteen incarnations — many, many, many, many incarnations I am in exile living like a mere mortal. After having many, many hard knocks life after life, I realized that my kingdom is not this. This world is full of challenges — “samsara dukkha sagara” – so that blissful kingdom is within. I want that, which I lost. Pandavas mere asking for the kingdom did not work because Kauravas sitting here denied.
Similarly, my mere asking, my own divinity, is not adequate. because there are Kauruvas sitting in me who are denying me my kingdom. Who are these Kauruvas? Ahamkara — ego, desires, pride, jealousy, habits, greed, attachments. These are all various characteristics I have – negative characteristics. As long as they are there, I cannot get back my kingdom. And they are there – Kauruvas.
In the book, “God Talks With Arjuna,” Guruji explains, Duryodhana represents the King Material Desire in me. Duhshasana, his brother, represents anger. Karna represents attachment and greed. Bhishma represents ego, Dronacharya — habit, Shalya — pride. These are all Kauruvas sitting in me.
I have a bit of all these things — negative qualities; but I also have some Pandavas. Self-control – Arjuna. I have some degree of self-control. Arjuna is in me. Pranayama – Bhima, Yama-Niyama I follow. Nakula Sahadeva – they are here. Like that I have some Pandavas, too. So, it’s a war between my good tendencies and evil tendencies. As Arjuna was upset when he saw the people he had to fight, he said that it is not worth fighting my own people, not worth — I don’t need this material kingdom. I don’t want to fight!. Then Bhagavan Krishna advises that those whom you think that they’re your well-wishers, they are not truly your well-wishers. They are denying you, your rightful kingdom. Similarly, for me, to get back my Divinity I have to get rid of all these negative tendencies. But when I see the tendencies I have to relinquish I get alarmed. because I enjoy being lazy. I take pride in my position, in my possessions. Do I have to leave all these things?. I cannot enjoy anymore my sleep, laziness, this, that? No, it’s not worth!. Gurudeva, Paramahansa Yoganandaji, explains clearly that these negative tendencies are not going to give you permanent happiness. Your pride is not going to give you permanent happiness. Ego, desires, all these things one day you have to relinquish them. The process of relinquishing involves a battle, a struggle – Kurukshetra. That is what we are going to discuss.
With this, you know now, I’m not so much interested in that Kurukshetra war which took place some three thousand years ago somewhere out there in Haryana. I’m more concerned and interested about the Kurukshetra war that is taking place within me. Right here, right now — it’s taking place within me because I want divine kingdom. I want my rightful heritage. But for that, I have to fight this Kurukshetra war. I mean, that is the context we have to understand. Clearly outlining, the Gita’s balanced path of meditation and right activity, Paramahansa Yoganandaji shows how we can create for ourselves a life of spiritual integrity, serenity, simplicity and joy. Through our awakened intuition, we come to know the right course to take at every crossroad on the path of life. That is very important for me. The guidance of Gita is not only for self-realization, it is also to take the right course of action at every crossroad in my life. It gives guidance for day-to-day life, day-to-day living. The Assurance of God and the Necessity of Winning Paramahansa Yoganandaji gives a grand assurance. Beautiful! He wrote: “As God talked with Arjuna, so will He talk with you.”. We know that Bhagavan Krishna talked to Arjuna. God, in the form of Krishna, talked to Arjuna. “As God talked with Arjuna, so He will talk with you. As He lifted up the spirit and consciousness of Arjuna, so will He uplift you. As He granted Arjuna supreme spiritual vision, so will He confer enlightenment on you.". Why? Because God has no favourites. If God gave enlightenment to Arjuna, He will give to me too, if only I want it, if only I work for it. That is the assurance.
Guruji also says, “Each person has to fight his own battle of Kurukshetra.”. We’re all well aware of it; We’re all fighting on a day-to-day basis. “Each person has to fight his own battle of Kurukshetra. It’s a war not only worth winning, but in the divine order of the universe and of the eternal relationship between the soul and God, a war that, sooner or later, must be won.”. So, it’s a war, not only worth winning, but by God’s design, this is a war that must be won, sooner or later. Let it be sooner. It is not a question that I am going to — whether I’m going to win this battle? No, it’s a question “When?”. The words of Bhagawan Krishna to Arjuna in the Gita are at once, a profound scripture on the science of yoga, and a textbook for everyday living. That is more important for us now. It’s a textbook for everyday living. Why should we understand Gita, study Gita? Here is the reason. Paramahansaji says: “The underlying essential truths of all great world scriptures can find common amity in the infinite wisdom of the Gita’s mere 700 concise verses. The entire knowledge of the cosmos is packed into the Gita. Wherever one is on the way back to God, the Gita will shed its light on that segment of the journey.”. Isn’t it beautiful?. It’s for everyone — beginners, veterans, and those who are somewhere in the middle. “Wherever one is on the way back to God, the Gita will shed its light on that segment of the journey.”. Everyone, any time, can be benefited.
One thing we have to understand, because this is a dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna, Guruji advises us, “Whenever Arjuna asks questions of God, it is to be understood that the meditating devotee by silent thoughts is communing with God.”. It is not that out there something is happening between Arjuna and Krishna. No! It is happening between me and God. That Arjuna in me! Arjuna is there in me, Arjuna devotee — he’s communing. The Threefold Meaning of the Gita and the Bodies Next. The threefold meaning of the Gita: – material, astral, and spiritual. See, man has three bodies: physical, astral, and causal bodies. To understand this, incarnate man — that is you and me — is encased in a physical body of inert matter which is animated by a subtle inner astral body of life energy and sensory powers. And both these physical and astral bodies have evolved from still subtler body, causal – causal body. To demonstrate this, I used a glove last time. Suppose if I put on a glove to my hand and move. And glove is moving — that’s all what you see — glove is moving, but glove cannot move on its own. Glove is moving because my fingers are moving. My fingers are moving because of the instructions they receive from my thought. The glove is inert matter; on its own it cannot move — that is physical body. Physical body – inert matter, can’t move. That is operated by astral body — equivalent to the fingers – astral body of life energy and the sensory powers. And even fingers are moving because of the instructions received from the thought. That is causal body. Causal body operating fingers; fingers, in turn, operating glove. So physical, astral and causal body – we have three bodies. In this overview, Bhagavad Gita gives instructions for all these, at all these levels, so that we are benefitted. All-round benefit we can get from this invaluable book, “God Talks with Arjuna.”. “In this overview, the material interpretation of the Gita pertains to the physical and social duties and well-being of man.”. Physical duties, social duties, and general well-being of man. I mean these are at body level – physical. “The astral is from the moral and psychological standpoint – man’s character resulting from the astral Nature-born sensory and life-energy principles that influence the formation of habits, inclinations and desires.”. So, my physical actions, that is one way — physical interpretation, material interpretation. Then the samskaras, my inclinations, the habits — that is astral level. Guidance is given, the psychological guidance is given. And finally, “the spiritual interpretation is from the perspective of the divine nature and realization of the soul.”. So even at that level we can get guidance from “God Talks With Arjuna”: physical, astral and spiritual. So that is the introduction to this book, “God Talks With Arjuna.”.
data.the-second-sloka-desire-approaches-habit:
Now we will go to the second sloka. Before we start the explanation let us listen to the second sloka sung by Sw. Vasudevanandaji.
“saṁjaya uvāca: dṛṣṭvā tu pāṇḍavānīkaṁ vyūḍhaṁ duryodhanas tadā ācāryam upasaṁgamya rājā vacanam abravīt. dṛṣṭvā tu pāṇḍavānīkaṁ vyūḍhaṁ duryodhanas tadā ācāryam upasaṁgamya rājā vacanam abravīt”.
The plain meaning of this second sloka, goes like this: “Sanjaya said: Then King Duryodhana, after having seen the armies of the Pandavas in battle array repaired to his preceptor (Drona), and spoke as follows:”. Look at the continuity. Dhritarashtra asked Sanjaya, “What is happening on the battlefield?”. In response to that question, Sanjaya said: “King Duryodhana, after having seen the armies of Pandavas, he approached his guru, Dronacharya and spoke as follows”. That’s all.
And many interpretations of Gita do not give much importance to this. It’s just like a fact, which was, of course, in a way. Duryodhana, having surveyed the armies of the enemies, approached his Acharya — Dronacharya to explain. But Guruji has gone deep into this. Metaphysical explanation is given which is very much applicable to you, and to me, in daily life. Duryodhana represents desire. Desire in me is Duryodhana. Dronacharya represents habit, samskara, inclinations – Dronacharya, past habit.
data.the-story-of-drupada-and-dronacharya#The:
Now, I will go to story, story of Drupada, Dhrishtadyumna, and Dronacharya. Dronacharya and Drupada were friends in the beginning. When Dronacharya needed material help, Drupada did not help, and Dronacharya felt humiliated. He took revenge by training Pandavas and asking them, as Guru Dakshina, to catch and imprison Drupada. Eventually, Drupada was caught as a prisoner by Dronacharya’s disciples.
When we start meditation initially, my habits also tend to help — initial enthusiasm. I start enjoying it. Automatically, I develop some vairagya, some dispassion and disinterest in normal activities. That means my sincere effort is helped, cooperated by my habits, also. But after some time, the habit sees that, “Oh, if he’s going, continuing in this direction, I’m going to be starved”. So, it rebels. After initial enthusiasm, our past habits overtake and kill that interest in meditation. Our past bad habits come back and catch us so that we leave our spiritual practices.
In the Mahabharata story, Drupada did not take it easily. He did very vigorous tapas, very vigorous spiritual practices with the sole aim of having a son who would kill Dronacharya with revenge. From that fire, Dhrishtadyumna comes out. He was blessed with a son coming from fire.
Similarly, after starting meditation, our old habits, bad habits, especially, overpower us, dissuade us. We have to develop that inner awakening. Somehow, we have to go on doing some kind of practices. Then comes that intuitive awakening, which can really conquer our bad habits. That’s how Dronacharya was killed eventually — because of tapas done by Drupada. Similarly, I will definitely conquer all my lower nature, all my negative tendencies, by involving with resolute determination in meditation and other spiritual practices. Overcoming Bad Habits
The man who is always restless and who never meditates believes that he is ‘all right’. He realizes the true plight as soon as spiritual desire awakens in him and he tries to meditate and be calm. He then naturally meets fierce resistance from the bad habits of mental fickleness. To watch some movie for three hours, I sit before a TV, surrender to TV. Next two hours you can be there watching — watching news — no problem of concentration. But you go and sit in meditation, fifteen minutes is a big struggle. That is why we are finding it difficult to meditate — meditate initially.
Guruji’s advice: “It is much more difficult for the occult soldiers in reclaiming the kingdom of peace once it has fallen into the hands of King Material Desire. One, therefore, must make the most of his spiritual inclination while the forces of his willingness to meditate are strong. It is good to start meditation at an early age; or, failing that, to start meditation on a regular daily schedule as soon as the mental discriminative inclination develops.”.
Once we realize that spiritual pursuits are very important for a human being, then immediately start the spiritual practices like meditation. It’s never too late to start, although it is more and more difficult, but never too late. Guruji gives a beautiful summary of third sloka. Thus, it is explained in this verse that when Material Desire and his army of sense tendencies and their restless thoughts try to reinforce themselves by Past Material Habit in order to dissuade the spiritual aspirant from the practice of meditation, they find that the Calm Inner Light of awakening intuition, well trained in meditation by Past Spiritual Habit, has effectively arrayed the discriminative faculties to give metaphysical resistance.
By nature, every devotee has that inner urge to progress spiritually by sadhana. But unfortunately, the habits of procrastination, laziness, tendency for instant material gratifications — sense gratifications — they oppose, they dissuade, because we want instant happiness. So, lie on the bed, instant happiness; sit before the TV, instant happiness; take a phone call, instant pleasure. These things dissuade us although inside we are interested to do something noble, something higher.

data.correlation-with-patanjali-yoga-sutras-a:
here there is perfect analogy with Patanjali Yoga Sutras. we have seen that the good tendencies in us perfectly correlate with the tendencies given in Patanjali Yoga Sutras; they correlate very well. here even the negative tendencies are also mentioned in Patanjali Yoga Sutras.
Yoga Sutra 24 in Chapter 1 of Patanjali Yoga Sutras reads like this: Patanjali says “The lord is untouched by klesha meaning trouble, karma action, vipaka habit, ashaya desire”. meaning Lord is beyond these qualities—troubles, action, habit and desire—He doesn’t have.
In another yoga sutra, Sutra 3 in the second chapter, the klesha (trouble) is defined as fivefold: avidya meaning ignorance, asmita meaning ego, raga attachment, dwisha aversion, avinivesa body attachment. thus here there are eight qualities are mentioned which Lord is untouched by, meaning Lord doesn’t have these defects. these imperfections are completely away from God like material action and habit and desire, ignorance, ego, attachment, repulsion—He doesn’t have.
What is that we are looking for in our life? self-realization, our lasting happiness, meaning I am God, I am a spark of divinity. if I am divine, I must be having all the qualities of God in me. what are the qualities of God? love, joy, wisdom, compassion, forgiveness. these are the qualities of Lord so all these qualities I must have. similarly God doesn’t have certain qualities like ego, habit, desires, attachment, repulsion. these qualities God doesn’t have so I also should be free from these imperfections if I were to become God. now ahambramasmi is the fundamental truth, I am divine. if so I must be having this good qualities in me and I must be having none of these bad qualities. but if I honestly look within I have these imperfections in me. I have desire, repulsion, attachment, likes, dislikes, all these I have. The question is: are you going to get rid of these infections when you become God, or you become God when you get rid of these imperfections? the answer is clear: my sadhana means I have to get rid of these imperfections in me. when these imperfections are out of my system, my consciousness, then I am that close to divinity.
Sadhana means that, as Yoganandaji said in one sentence: “seeking God means expressing God”. if I say that I am a devotee, I am seeking God, means I must be expressing God in my daily life. I must be expressing love, joy, forgiveness, compassion, wisdom. at the same time I should not have any imperfections like ego, raga, dwisha, attachment, repulsion, desires. that is what is meant by sadhana. Remember that seeking God means expressing God. we must live like that, not only for the sake of achieving God’s self-realization, but even for lasting happiness. if you have these imperfections—ego, delusion, desires, raga, dwesha—then we can’t be happy in life.

What do they represent? data.summary-of-evil-tendencies#Summary of Ev:

Krupacharya (individual delusion/illusion/avidya). Bhishma (ego). Karna (raga/like/attachment). Vikarna (dwesha/repulsion/dislike). Son of Somadatta (material action). data.the-first-sloka-life-is-a-series-of-batt: with this background we studied the first loka of the first chapter in Gita. the first sloka tells us a fundamental truth that life is a series of battles between good and evil, knowledge and ignorance, soul and body, self-control and temptation and the like. it’s constantly going on. The advice given to us by Veda Vyasa is that a devotee each night should honestly introspect, like Sanjay was describing what was happening on the battlefield to blind king Dhritarashtra. our introspection should reveal to our mind how our bad tendencies and good tendencies were on that day. we have to introspect each day. it is not that we want to know what we have done, more importantly, we want to know why we did what we did, what is the purpose, what is the motive behind our actions. that is also important if we are to progress spiritually. that is the import of the first loka.
data.the-second-sloka-warning-against-materia:
the second sloka gives us a warning how our past bad habits try to dissipate when we start spiritual practices. thus we find the second verse of the Gita forewarning the spiritual aspirant that king Duryodhana (material desire) will try to arouse man’s Dronacharya (sense habit tendencies) to fight against the sole forces of discrimination. an ordinary person knowing nothing about the supreme joy that can come out of meditation innocently reconciles himself to sense pleasures whatever he can get through tongue, eyes, ears—he’s happy. but once he starts meditating and he finds that there is so much more in this meditation, then the king material desire inside, which was always depending on the senses for its pleasures, gets alarmed. this fellow is now going towards meditation, that means I would be denied of my joys which I was getting from all these senses all along. so he would turn towards Dronacharya (past habit) to discourage the devotee from meditating.
That’s why we find that whenever we sit in meditation, especially in the beginning, we get so many reminders of the unfinished jobs to dissuade us from meditating. thoughts like “oh you have to make a telephone call,” or “that incomplete job first, right now finish and then you can meditate peacefully,” or “others are waiting for dinner,” or “you are tired, tomorrow you can see,” come to discourage the person. even those persons with resolute effort who sit for meditation then the past habit of sleepiness, thoughts, all these things also try to dissuade him. so this is the warning given to us: beware, beware, discouragement doesn’t necessarily come from outside, others disturbing us; discouragement comes from within most of the time.
data.the-third-sloka-the-role-of-intuitive-aw:
